job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Beth Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at eight at Crestmoor Bank, in loan operations. I check documents for small business loans, matching figures, flagging gaps, and sending files to the analysts. After work I study for the first level of the CFA, which is an investment qualification, and on Sundays I help at my parents' takeaway in Dunmore. I did a finance degree and passed, with no internships, and I live in a rented flat with a friend from uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right, and a bit of a relief. At work I'd tell my teammates that the new document checker is nice but it doesn't change much. With friends I'd say we've been hearing about the end of jobs for years and I'll believe it when I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm happy to have an ordinary career. I'm in loan operations at Crestmoor Bank, checking documents for small business loans. It's steady, the bank is stable, and I can see a path to a junior analyst role in two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the work and keep studying for the first level of the CFA, which is an investment qualification, on weekday evenings. I'd put 150 a month on my loan and save 150. I'd also keep helping my parents at their takeaway on Sunday evenings, because they're short-staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. I'm not rich, but I'm in a decent spot for 22.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the merger last spring. What did you see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd watch is the bank's headcount. Crestmoor merged two branches last spring, and some people went. Bank cuts happen with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the Sunday shifts at the takeaway fit with your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a cut came, I'd want to already have the CFA level one done. It makes a CV look serious. And if that failed, my parents' takeaway would always give me a few shifts.

say: I'd say it's **about right**, since we've heard about the end of jobs for years.
At work I'd say the document checker is nice but doesn't change much.
think: I'm happy to have an **ordinary career** with a path to analyst in two or three years.
The bank's **headcount** is the real risk, with or without AI.
do: Keep studying for **CFA level one** on weekday evenings.
Put **150 a month** on my loan and save 150.
Help at my parents' **takeaway** on Sunday evenings.
feel: I'd feel **settled**, in a decent spot for 22.
S0.quote: Bank cuts happen with or without AI.
fieldNote: Beth's calm is based on a **stable bank**, though last spring's branch merger shows cuts happen anyway.
Her backup is concrete: the **CFA** exam on her CV and shifts at her parents' takeaway.

steps.text: Study for CFA level one on weekday evenings
Save 150 a month and put 150 on the loan
Keep working Sunday shifts at my parents' takeaway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably going to be real, and we should be sensible. At work I'd say let's learn the new tools before they're put on us. With friends I'd say don't panic, but pay attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, loan document checking is the sort of thing that goes first. Reading forms, matching figures, flagging gaps. I use AI tools now and then for drafting emails, but the bank's version will go much further, and the team is eleven people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager, Tomasz, if I can be part of the pilot for the bank's checking tool, so I'm one of the people who knows it. I'd keep studying for the CFA and add a short course in credit analysis, around 250. I'd also move my savings plan to 250 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little tense. I can handle change when it's proven, but this is moving faster than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the checking team was cut from eleven to seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pilot cuts the checking team to seven, I'd want to be one of the seven, or already moved to credit analysis. My parents would say take any job in a bank. I'd say I'm trying, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you believe the bank would retrain people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to think the bank will retrain people rather than cut. The people above me say that, but then I remember what happened to the merged branches. So I plan as if the bank won't retrain people.

say: I'd say we should learn the tools **before** they're put on us.
I'd tell friends **don't panic**, but pay attention.
think: Loan document checking is the kind of work that goes **first**, and my team is eleven people.
I plan as if the bank **won't** retrain people.
do: Ask Tomasz to join the bank's **pilot** of the checking tool.
Add a short **credit analysis** course, around 250.
feel: I feel a bit **tense**, since this is moving faster than proven.
S1.quote: I plan as if the bank won't retrain people.
fieldNote: Beth acts as a **steady** adopter: she asks to join the pilot so she knows the tool before it is imposed.
She does not trust the bank's **retraining** promises, remembering the branch merger.

steps.text: Ask Tomasz to put me on the checking tool pilot
Take a short credit analysis course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short for anyone to cope, and we need public help, not just promises. At work I'd ask the bank what the plan is. With friends I'd talk about how our whole degree might be pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job goes in about a year and a half. The CFA wouldn't save me, because a machine would do analysis too. I'd be on the same footing as anyone else with a finance degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I could and save 400 a month. I'd ask Mum and Dad if I could move back above the takeaway in Dunmore if my job ended, which would cut my rent to nothing. I'd drop the CFA, since it costs around 1,000 and might lead nowhere, and I'd learn how to cook and manage the takeaway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, with a big sense of unfairness. I played by the rules and did the degree and the exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean for you to work at your parents' takeaway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's odd, but the takeaway looks safer than the bank to me in that world. A person cooking and serving is harder to replace until the robots arrive. That's about three years later. It would buy me time, and my parents would be happy to have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Hana use each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also talk to my friend Hana, who is in her second year at a graduate scheme. If she hears anything at her firm, we'd swap news. In a fast change, you want people who tell you things straight.

say: I'd say two years is **too short** for anyone to cope, and we need public help.
I'd ask the bank what the **plan** is.
think: My job goes in about **18 months**, and the CFA wouldn't save me.
I played by the rules, and it feels **unfair**.
do: Save **400 a month** and drop the roughly 1,000 CFA fee.
Move back above the **takeaway** in Dunmore if my job ends.
Learn to **manage** the takeaway with my parents.
feel: I'd be **scared**, with a strong sense of unfairness.
S2.quote: A person cooking and serving is harder to replace until the robots arrive.
fieldNote: Beth sees her family's **takeaway** as safer than the bank, because hands-on work gets about three more years.
She drops the **CFA** because she expects machines to do analysis too.

steps.text: Drop the CFA and save 400 a month
Move above the takeaway in Dunmore if laid off
Learn to run the takeaway with my parents
Swap job news with friend Hana each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good heads-up, and the people in charge should use it. At work I'd say the bank must be open about its plans. With friends I'd say keep your options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm probably going to be okay, but it won't be the career I pictured. I'd have to find a corner of finance that needs trust and judgement, or a different field. Five years is just enough to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish CFA level one and two over the next two years, because I'd want to test whether the qualification keeps its value. At the same time I'd do a short course in data skills and start using the AI tools every week. I'd save 300 a month and keep Sundays at the takeaway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like a long runway with a lot of fog. Not scary every day, but always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test whether the CFA keeps its value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year two I'd decide. If the bank was laying people off, I'd move on to a smaller firm or take a customer-facing role, where trust matters. I'd tell my parents about it over a Sunday meal so no one is surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents on that Sunday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also keep my ear on the ground. My manager Tomasz is straight with me, and he'd say if there's a problem. I'd treat that as my early warning.

say: I'd say five years is a good **heads-up**, and the people in charge should use it.
I'd say the bank must be **open** about its plans.
think: I'll probably be **okay**, but not in the career I pictured.
I need a corner of finance that needs **trust and judgement**.
do: Finish **CFA** level one and two over two years to test their value.
Take a short **data skills** course and use AI tools weekly.
Save **300 a month** and keep Sundays at the takeaway.
feel: It feels like a long runway with a lot of **fog**.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a long runway with a lot of fog.
fieldNote: Beth uses the five years to **test** the qualification and learn tools weekly, a very steady-adopter move.
She relies on her manager Tomasz as an **early warning** source.

steps.text: Sit CFA level one and two over two years
Use the bank's AI tools every week
Move to a customer-facing role in year two if layoffs start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and that's good news. At work I'd carry on. With friends I'd say it's the time to get skilled at something durable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be calm. I'd be 32, with a few years in finance, a qualification, and some savings. I'd try to be someone who works with the tools, not against them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the CFA, move up to analyst or relationship roles, and build savings at 300 a month, aiming for a deposit by 28. I'd learn the AI tools as they mature, step by step. I'd also keep up a bit of cooking at the takeaway for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. Ten years lets me change my mind a couple of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the yearly review look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My one fear is that I get comfortable and wake up in year eight with nothing new. I'd put a yearly review in my diary to check that I'm still moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the ten years turned out to be shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI came sooner than ten years, I'd feel cheated, but I'd have savings and a skill or two. That's a decent cushion at that point.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, and it's the time to get skilled at something durable.
think: I'd be **calm**, at 32 with a qualification, experience and savings.
I'd try to work **with** the tools, not against them.
do: Finish the **CFA** and move up to analyst or relationship roles.
Save **300 a month** toward a deposit by 28.
Learn AI tools **step by step** as they mature.
feel: I'd be **quite calm**, since ten years lets me change my mind a couple of times.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me change my mind a couple of times.
fieldNote: Beth is **calm** because a decade lets her change course twice and still have savings.
Her one fear is **comfort**, so she plans a yearly review.

steps.text: Finish the CFA and aim for an analyst role
Save 300 a month toward a deposit by 28
Learn the bank's AI tools step by step
Hold a yearly review of my career in my diary

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. My job and my qualification are both desk-based, and two years isn't time to move. What would help is open talk from the bank about its plans, public support for retraining, and good cash savings. My parents' takeaway is my safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people my age aren't lazy and aren't naive. We did what we were told, with a degree, an exam, a first job. What's being asked now is a different game, and we'd need help playing it.

headlineQuote: We did what we were told, with a degree, an exam, a first job.
portrait: Beth is a finance graduate, four months into loan operations at a bank, **renting** with a friend from university.
She is a centrist and uses AI tools now and then, so she prefers to join pilots rather than be surprised.
Her mood moves from calm to **anxious** as warning time shortens, and she plans around the CFA and her parents' takeaway.
She sees the takeaway as a **safety net** because hands-on work gets about three more years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most: both her job and her CFA study are desk work, and two years is too short.
whatWouldHelp: Open talk from the bank, public **retraining**, savings, and her parents' takeaway as a fallback.
